questions.q: Describe the position of peasants and zamindars in Mughal agrarian society.
answer: Agrarian society under the Mughals, known chiefly from the Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl, rested on the peasants who tilled the land and the zamindars who stood above them.

answer.text: The peasant, called the raiyat, was the backbone of rural society. There were two kinds: the khud-kashta, who were resident cultivators owning land in their own village, and the pahi-kashta, who were non-resident cultivators coming from other villages. Peasants grew both food crops and valuable cash crops, and their work was organised through the village community and its panchayat.

The zamindars were landed proprietors who enjoyed high social status. They held their own lands, called milkiyat, and, more importantly, collected land revenue from the peasants on behalf of the state, keeping a share for themselves. Many maintained armed retainers and forts.

answer: Thus peasants produced the wealth of the land, while zamindars linked them to the Mughal state.

questions.q: How was the Mughal land revenue system organised, and why was it central to the empire?

answer.text: was the economic foundation of the Mughal Empire, so its collection was carefully organised.

list: The state claimed a share of the produce of the land, assessed and usually collected in cash
Officials measured land and classified it by fertility to fix the revenue, a system developed under Akbar and his minister Todar Mal

answer.lead: It was central to the empire.

list: It paid for the army, the court and the administration that held the vast empire together
Because so much depended on it, the Mughals kept detailed records and a large body of revenue officials

questions.q: What was the role of the village community and the panchayat in Mughal rural society?

answer.text: was the basic unit of rural society in Mughal India, and it enjoyed a large measure of self-management.

list: The village community included peasants of different status, artisans and menial workers
It largely managed its own affairs, including local disputes and shared resources

answer.text: It was an assembly of village elders.

list: Headed by a headman (muqaddam or mandal), it collected revenue, settled disputes and upheld customs
It also looked after the welfare of the community and its dealings with the state and the zamindar
